nodeData.topic:
🟢 Biliary Tract
Anatomy, Physiology &
Surgical Clinical Anatomy

children.topic:
I. Gross Anatomy —
Gallbladder

Pear-shaped, on visceral surface of liver;
~7.5–12.5 cm, capacity ~50 mL

Four segments:
fundus → body → infundibulum → neck → cystic duct

Fundus at tip of 9th costal cartilage /
lateral rectus border; fully peritonealized

Hartmann's pouch = dilated infundibulum;
not universal — found in 12.2% of gallbladders

Cystic duct 1–3 cm, mucosal spiral valves of Heister;
conventional cystic duct anatomy in 89%

Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses =
mucosal outpouchings

Ducts of Luschka = subvesical bile ducts
in the cystic plate ⚠️ (bile leak source)

II. Gross Anatomy —
Extrahepatic Ducts / CBD

Right hepatic duct = anterior + posterior sectoral ducts;
left = medial + lateral

Variants: right posterior duct into
left hepatic duct 16%; triple confluence 12%

CHD ~4 cm → CBD 8–10 cm long, 5–6 mm diameter
(up to 8 mm)

Four parts:
supraduodenal → retroduodenal → intrapancreatic → intraduodenal

Portal triad rule: CBD anterolateral right,
hepatic artery left, portal vein posterior

Terminates at ampulla of Vater, major papilla,
D2, encircled by sphincter of Oddi
III. Vascular Supply

Cystic artery from right hepatic artery in 83.6%;
other origins 16.4%

Duplicate cystic artery 7.18%; aberrant supply
seen in up to 57% of CVS photos

Bile duct supply is axial — 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock arteries;
plus retroportal artery (major contributor in 32%)

⚠️ Circumferential/lateral dissection of the supraduodenal duct
→ ischemic, long strictures

Venous: multiple small veins to liver bed + cystic vein
→ right portal branch (does not parallel artery)
IV. Triangles

Hepatocystic triangle: cystic duct (inferior),
CHD (medial), inferior liver surface (superior)

Calot's original triangle: CHD (base),
cystic duct (inferior), cystic artery (superior)

Contents: cystic artery, cystic node of Lund,
± aberrant right hepatic duct (1.03%)

Critical View of Safety > triangle dogma:
cleared triangle, lower third of cystic plate exposed,
only 2 structures entering gallbladder

V. Variations
(High-Yield)

Moynihan's hump / caterpillar turn of RHA:
cadaveric/imaging 1.8%; intraoperative series 6.26% ⚠️ vulnerable to ligation

Phrygian cap — kinked fundal fold,
benign, mimics pathology on imaging

Cystic duct: low insertion 11.2%,
medial insertion 9.8%, parallel course 7.4%

"Normal" textbook pattern present
in only 57–72%

Embryologic basis: caudal bud → gallbladder/cystic duct;
over-migration → intrahepatic GB, lag → floating GB
VI. Physiology
Hepatic bile secretion ~40 mL/hr (continuous)

GB concentrates bile 5–10× by absorbing
water, Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃⁻; secretes ~20 mL/day mucus

CCK from duodenal I-cells (fat/AA) →
GB contraction + sphincter of Oddi relaxation

Cholangiocytes actively modify bile:
add HCO₃⁻ and mucin, reabsorb water/chloride

VII. Clinical Syndromes,
Pearls & Connections
Clinical Anatomy Syndromes
Incidence danger = CHD mistaken for cystic duct → bile duct injury

Bouveret syndrome = gastric outlet obstruction
from stone impacted in duodenum
"Lost" spilled stones → delayed intra-abdominal abscess
Pearls / Red Flags
⚠️ Never dissect at 3 and 9 o'clock on the CBD

⚠️ Any "third element" in the hepatocystic triangle =
stop and reassess (posterior cystic artery, caterpillar hump, aberrant RHD)

Jaundice + cholecystitis picture → think Mirizzi,
image with MRCP before laparoscopy

Pneumobilia without prior instrumentation/ERCP
→ biliary-enteric fistula
Connections

Mirizzi ↔ gallstone ileus ↔ Bouveret —
one pathophysiologic continuum from an impacted infundibular stone
(pressure necrosis → fistula), differing only in where the fistula drains

3-and-9-o'clock arteries ↔ post-cholecystectomy
and post-transplant strictures — the same ischemic mechanism
explains anastomotic strictures after Whipple and liver transplant

Differential trap: Phrygian cap, adenomyomatosis septations,
and a folded gallbladder on ultrasound can mimic wall thickening
or a mass — and a caterpillar-hump RHA can be mistaken for the cystic artery
